Unfold `disjointed` as the residual
\[
\operatorname{disjointed}(f)(i)=f(i)\setminus\bigvee_{j<i}f(j).
\]

At the bottom element, the strict lower interval is empty, so the removed supremum is \(0\); hence `disjointed f 0 = f 0`.

For the second conjunct, interpret joins of sets as unions and `partialSups f n` as
\[
\bigcup_{i\le n} f(i).
\]
One inclusion is immediate since every residual piece lies in its original set. For the reverse inclusion, given \(x\in f(i)\) with \(i\le n\), choose a minimal index \(j\le i\) such that \(x\in f(j)\). Such a \(j\) exists because `Iic i` is finite. Minimality says \(x\notin f(k)\) for every \(k<j\), so \(x\in\operatorname{disjointed}(f)(j)\), with \(j\le n\). Thus the union of all disjointed pieces below \(n\) recovers the partial supremum.

The essential assumption is local finiteness below: it supplies the minimal supporting index.
